entries.title: Creole rémoulade
entries.summary: The New Orleans rémoulade is a cold, spiced sauce led by Creole mustard, with paprika, cayenne, horseradish, lemon, garlic, celery, green onion and parsley. Pinker and hotter than the French one, it is the sauce of shrimp rémoulade.
entries.guest: Creole rémoulade is a cool, tangy New Orleans sauce, often pink with paprika and sharp with Creole mustard. Ours is a chive rémoulade, cool and herby, for dipping the Crawfish Meat Pies.

paras: Rémoulade, said REM-uh-lahd (RUM-uh-lahd is heard in New Orleans), is a cold sauce for seafood and cold dishes. The New Orleans version is pink to brick red, hot and sharp. Creole mustard leads it: a coarse, stone-ground brown mustard with a vinegary bite. Paprika gives the colour, cayenne the heat, prepared horseradish a nose-clearing sting and lemon the brightness. Garlic, finely chopped celery, green onion and flat-leaf parsley bring crunch and freshness.

It matters because it is one of the sauces that taste of the city. Its great dish is shrimp rémoulade: chilled boiled shrimp dressed in the sauce and set on a bed of shredded iceberg lettuce, the cold, crisp lettuce cooling the heat.

There are two styles. The pink style is built on mayonnaise. For about 500 ml (2 cups) of sauce, start with 240 ml (1 cup) of mayonnaise and stir in 60 ml (4 tbsp) of Creole mustard, 15 ml (1 tbsp) of prepared horseradish, 5 g (2 tsp) of sweet paprika, the juice of half a lemon and one clove of garlic mashed to a paste with a pinch of salt. Add cayenne and hot sauce a pinch and a dash at a time. Fold in about 30 g (4 tbsp) each of finely chopped celery and green onion and about 8 g (2 tbsp) of chopped parsley, then salt to taste.

The red style has no mayonnaise at all. It is a dressing, close to a vinaigrette: Creole mustard, paprika, horseradish, lemon juice or vinegar and the seasonings are whisked together, then oil is whisked in until the mustard holds it in a loose, brick-red emulsion, meaning oil held in tiny droplets through the liquid. Work at about two parts oil to one part mustard, with the acid to taste. Some New Orleans kitchens still make it this way, and it eats hotter and leaner than the pink.

Either way, make it at least an hour ahead and chill it: the flavours marry and the paprika's colour deepens as it rests. Taste it again cold, because cold dulls salt and heat. Keep it covered at 5°C (41°F) or below, as you would any mayonnaise sauce, and dress the shrimp close to service so the lettuce stays crisp.

The French rémoulade, which has its own entry, is white: mayonnaise with mustard, chopped gherkins, capers, herbs and, in Escoffier, a little anchovy essence, close to a tartar sauce. The New Orleans sauce kept the name and went its own way: pinker from paprika, hotter from cayenne and horseradish, and led by mustard rather than by mayonnaise and pickles. Its close New Orleans cousin is ravigote, another cold, sharp sauce for crab and shrimp.

A flat, dull rémoulade lacks acid or salt, or was seasoned warm; add lemon and salt and taste it cold. A thin, weeping one was made with wet shrimp or celery, or is a red dressing whose emulsion has let go; dry everything well and whisk the dressing again with a spoonful of mustard. A harsh, bitter edge comes from old, dusty paprika or too much raw garlic, which sharpens as the sauce rests; use fresh paprika, mash the garlic to a paste with a pinch of salt and keep to one clove. A sauce too hot to taste anything else had its cayenne added in one go, so build the heat in pinches.

At Brennan's the sauce appears as a chive rémoulade with the Crawfish Meat Pies, a snack on the Bubbles at Brennan's list served in the Roost Bar and the courtyard: cool, tangy and herby against the hot pastry. The menu does not print the recipe, so whether it is the pink or the red style, and what goes into it, are questions for the kitchen. Rémoulade is also one of the five New Orleans sauces the courtyard turtles are named for, beside Ravigote, Bordelaise, Mignonette and Cocktail.

Describe the New Orleans sauce plainly: cool and tangy, pink with paprika, sharp with Creole mustard and horseradish. Warn a guest who expects the mild French or tartar-style sauce that the Creole one usually has heat. For the chive rémoulade on the meat pies, say cool, tangy and herby, and send questions about egg, mustard, heat or anything else in it to the kitchen, because the house recipe is not printed.

questions.answer: Pinker, hotter and led by mustard

entries.title: Ravigote, French and New Orleans
entries.summary: Ravigote is a sharp, herb-led sauce whose name means revived. In France it is a cold vinaigrette with capers, shallot and fines herbes, or a warm velouté sauce; in New Orleans it is lump crab in a cold, creamy dressing.
entries.guest: Ravigote means revived: a sharp sauce of capers, vinegar and herbs. In New Orleans it usually means lump crab in a cold, creamy dressing, sometimes baked hot.

paras: Ravigote, said rah-vee-GOHT, comes from the French verb ravigoter, to revive or perk up, and the sauce does what its name says: it wakes up a plain or rich food with acid, shallot and a handful of fresh herbs. It is not one recipe but three, and the menu line tells you which is meant.

The French kitchen has a cold ravigote, a vinaigrette for calf's head and cold meats, and a warm ravigote built on velouté. New Orleans has a third of its own: crabmeat ravigote, lump crab in a cold, mayonnaise-based dressing. All three share a sharp, acid edge and fresh herbs, and very little else; capers belong to the cold ones.

The cold French ravigote is a seasoned vinaigrette. Escoffier gives it among his cold sauces as an oil and vinegar dressing with small capers, finely chopped onion and the fines herbes, served with calf's head and calf's feet. Work at about three parts oil to one part wine vinegar. For 250 ml (about 1 cup) of sauce, whisk 60 ml (1/4 cup) of vinegar with salt and pepper, then whisk in 180 ml (3/4 cup) of oil.

Fold in about 10 g (1 tbsp) of small capers, rinsed and chopped, 15 ml (1 tbsp) of very finely chopped shallot or onion, and about 8 g (2 tbsp) of fines herbes: chervil, tarragon, chives and flat-leaf parsley, cut fine with a sharp knife so they stay green. Add the herbs within the hour of service, because vinegar dulls their colour as it sits. Spoon it over warm tête de veau, calf's head simmered and rolled, or over cold boiled beef, tongue or poached fish.

The warm ravigote is a different sauce again: a velouté, a stock sauce thickened with a pale roux, sharpened with wine and vinegar. It is taught under the velouté family and named here only so it is not mistaken for the cold ones.

New Orleans took the name and made it a crab dish. Crabmeat ravigote is lump blue crab folded into a cold dressing of mayonnaise sharpened with Creole mustard, capers, green onion, parsley and lemon. Mayonnaise has no place in the French ravigote; here it is the base. A working ratio is about 120 ml (1/2 cup) of dressing to 450 g (1 lb) of lump crab: enough to coat, never to drown.

It is served cold, mounded on lettuce, in a halved avocado or with toast points, as a starter in the city's old-line dining rooms. Some kitchens bake it: crab and dressing go into a ramekin or a cleaned crab shell under breadcrumbs and are heated until the edges bubble. Fold with a spatula, never stir, because lump crab is paid for by the size of its pieces. Keep the crab and the dressing at 5°C (41°F) or below until they are plated.

The faults follow the base. A cold French ravigote turns grey-green and flat when the herbs sit too long in the vinegar, and it separates into oil and vinegar if it is not whisked again before it is spooned. The crab ravigote fails when stirring breaks the lumps into shreds, when crab liquor makes the dressing weep, or when it is overdressed and tastes of mayonnaise rather than crab. A baked ravigote left too long turns oily as the mayonnaise breaks; take it out when the edges bubble.

Both French sauces are classical: Escoffier's A Guide to Modern Cookery, the 1907 English edition of his Guide Culinaire, gives a warm ravigote among the small sauces and a cold one, also called vinaigrette, among the cold sauces. The crab version came later, in the New Orleans restaurants, where mayonnaise, Creole mustard and Gulf crab made a French dressing local.

Which ravigote is on the plate? Read the menu line. Crabmeat ravigote is cold, creamy crab, sharp with mustard and capers, unless the menu says baked or the kitchen has said otherwise at lineup. On a French menu, calf's head or cold meats sauced ravigote come with the sharp herb vinaigrette; when it is the warm velouté, the kitchen will say so at lineup.

At Brennan's the word has a second life: Ravigote is one of the ten courtyard turtles, one of the five named for New Orleans sauces. Questions about shellfish, egg or mustard in any ravigote go to the kitchen.

cards.front: What does the French verb ravigoter mean, and what does the sauce do?
cards.back: To revive or perk up: a ravigote wakes up a plain or rich food with acid, shallot and fresh herbs.

cards.front: What are the three sauces called ravigote?
cards.back: The cold French vinaigrette, the warm French velouté sauce, and New Orleans crabmeat ravigote in a cold, creamy dressing.

cards.front: What goes into a cold French ravigote?
cards.back: Oil and wine vinegar at about three to one, with small capers, finely chopped shallot or onion and the fines herbes.

cards.front: Which herbs are the fines herbes, and when do they go into a cold ravigote?
cards.back: Chervil, tarragon, chives and parsley, cut fine and added within the hour of service so the vinegar does not grey them.

cards.front: What did Escoffier serve the cold ravigote with?
cards.back: Calf's head and calf's feet; it also suits cold boiled beef, tongue and poached fish, where its sharpness cuts richness.

cards.front: What is a warm ravigote?
cards.back: A velouté, a stock sauce on a pale roux, sharpened with wine and vinegar: a sauce of the velouté family, taught there, and not a dressing.

cards.front: What is New Orleans crabmeat ravigote?
cards.back: Lump crab folded into a cold mayonnaise dressing with capers, Creole mustard, green onion, parsley and lemon.

cards.front: Where does mayonnaise belong in ravigote?
cards.back: Only in the New Orleans crab ravigote; the French ravigote is a vinaigrette or a velouté sauce and takes no mayonnaise.

cards.front: Why is crab ravigote folded, never stirred?
cards.back: Lump crab is bought for the size of its pieces; stirring shreds it, so fold gently with a spatula and dress lightly.

cards.front: How does a baked crabmeat ravigote differ from the cold one?
cards.back: It goes into a ramekin or crab shell under breadcrumbs and is heated until the edges bubble; left too long, the mayonnaise turns oily.

cards.front: How does the word ravigote reach the Brennan's courtyard?
cards.back: Ravigote is one of the ten courtyard turtles, one of the five named for New Orleans sauces.

cards.front: How do you tell a guest which ravigote is on the plate?
cards.back: Read the menu line: crabmeat ravigote is cold, creamy crab unless it is baked; calf's head or cold meats sauced ravigote take the herb vinaigrette, and the kitchen says when it is the warm velouté.

entries.title: New Orleans barbecue shrimp
entries.say: As it reads: New Orleans barbecue shrimp.
entries.summary: New Orleans barbecue shrimp are never barbecued: head-on shrimp cooked in a peppery pan sauce of butter, Worcestershire, garlic and lemon. Credited to Pascal's Manale, the dish is eaten with the hands, a bib and plenty of bread.
entries.guest: Barbecue shrimp in New Orleans means no smoke and no tomato: shrimp cooked in butter with black pepper, garlic and lemon. Our Louisiana Oysters come in that sauce at breakfast and lunch.

paras: New Orleans barbecue shrimp is the city's quiet joke on visitors: nothing is barbecued, smoked or grilled, and there is no tomato. Large head-on Gulf shrimp are cooked in a pan sauce of butter, a heavy hand of black pepper, Worcestershire sauce, garlic and lemon, often with Creole seasoning, and some cooks add rosemary or hot sauce. The result is buttery, peppery and a deep reddish brown.

It matters because the word confuses guests every night. Anyone from outside Louisiana hears barbecue and expects smoke or a sweet red sauce. The server's first job is to say what it is before the plate lands.

The heads carry much of the flavour: the fat inside them melts into the butter and makes the sauce richer and deeper. For 450 g (1 lb) of large head-on shrimp, shells on, have ready 115 g (4 oz) of cold butter cut in cubes, 30 ml (2 tbsp) of Worcestershire, about 30 ml (2 tbsp) of lemon juice, three cloves of garlic, chopped, and 7 to 14 g (1 to 2 tbsp) of coarsely cracked black pepper.

Melt a knob of the butter in a wide pan over medium-high heat, add the garlic for a few seconds, then the shrimp in one layer. Add the Worcestershire, lemon, pepper and seasoning with a splash of shrimp stock or water, and turn the shrimp as they colour. Take them to nearly done, 2 to 4 minutes, the shells pink and the flesh turning opaque; they finish in the sauce, and seafood is cooked to 63°C (145°F). Do not crowd the pan, or the shrimp stew in their own water.

Then lower the heat and swirl in the cold butter a few cubes at a time, shaking the pan, until the liquid turns glossy and thick enough to coat a spoon; with a full pan or a slow hand, lift the shrimp into a warm bowl before the butter goes in, and pour the sauce over them. That is a pan emulsion: butter held in a little liquid, the idea behind a beurre blanc, burr BLAHN, the French butter sauce. Once the butter is in it must not boil, and it must not sit on the pass, the counter where finished plates wait for a server, or it splits into a pool of grease.

A greasy, split sauce boiled after the butter went in, or waited too long; off the heat, whisk in a spoonful of hot stock or water, and next time serve it straight away. Tight, rubbery shrimp were overcooked or left in the hot sauce; pull them when just opaque. Soft, mushy flesh means head-on shrimp were kept too long before cooking, because enzymes in the head soften the tail. A thin, pale sauce had too much liquid when the butter went in; reduce it first. A flat taste wants more pepper or more lemon: the dish is meant to be peppery, and the lemon keeps the butter from cloying.

The dish is credited to Pascal's Manale, an Uptown restaurant on Napoleon Avenue. By the family's account, in 1954, though some tellings say 1953, a regular described a buttery, peppery shrimp dish he had eaten in Chicago, and the kitchen worked out its own version, which he liked better. Tell it as their story; why it took the name barbecue has never been settled.

This is a dish eaten with the hands. Bring a bib, extra napkins, a bowl for shells and plenty of hot French bread, because the sauce is the point and the bread is how a guest eats it. Show a guest new to head-on shrimp how to twist off the head, peel the tail and, if they like, suck the head for its juices. Describe it as buttery and peppery, rich rather than hot.

Brennan's uses the name on two plates. The Louisiana Oysters, a breakfast and lunch starter, are oysters in the buttery, peppery sauce with pickled collard greens, shallots and a fried saltine crumble; how they are cooked and plated is confirmed at lineup. The Louisiana BBQ Lobster, the second course of the dinner tasting, gives lobster the same treatment over a white bean stew with ’nduja, en-DOO-yah, a soft, spicy pork sausage from Calabria. The house recipe is not published, so describe it as a buttery, peppery New Orleans BBQ sauce, and send questions about the Worcestershire, traditionally made with anchovy, or anything else in it to the kitchen.

cards.front: Why is New Orleans barbecue shrimp not barbecue?
cards.back: It is never smoked or grilled and has no tomato: head-on shrimp cook in a pan sauce of butter, black pepper, Worcestershire, garlic and lemon.

cards.front: Why are barbecue shrimp cooked with their heads on?
cards.back: The fat in the heads melts into the butter and makes the sauce richer and deeper.

cards.front: How much butter goes with 450 g (1 lb) of head-on shrimp?
cards.back: About 115 g (4 oz) of cold butter in cubes, with 30 ml (2 tbsp) each of Worcestershire and lemon juice.

cards.front: What should barbecue shrimp taste of first?
cards.back: Butter and black pepper: the dish is peppery rather than hot, and the lemon keeps the butter from cloying.

cards.front: What kind of sauce is barbecue shrimp sauce?
cards.back: A pan emulsion: cold butter swirled into a little hot liquid, off the boil, until it turns glossy and coats a spoon.

cards.front: What breaks a barbecue shrimp sauce?
cards.back: Boiling after the butter goes in, or sitting on the pass; it splits into grease, so it is finished and served at once.

cards.front: How do you know the shrimp are done?
cards.back: Taken nearly done in 2 to 4 minutes, they finish in the sauce: shells pink, flesh just opaque; seafood is cooked to 63°C (145°F).

cards.front: Where was barbecue shrimp born, by the family's account?
cards.back: At Pascal's Manale, Uptown on Napoleon Avenue, in 1954, after a regular described a shrimp dish he had eaten in Chicago.

cards.front: What does a guest need for barbecue shrimp?
cards.back: A bib, extra napkins, a bowl for the shells and plenty of hot French bread for the sauce.

cards.front: Which Brennan's dishes use the New Orleans barbecue sauce?
cards.back: The Louisiana Oysters at breakfast and lunch, and the Louisiana BBQ Lobster on the dinner tasting.

cards.front: Where do questions about the Worcestershire in the house sauce go?
cards.back: To the kitchen: the house recipe is not published, and Worcestershire is traditionally made with anchovy.

questions.q: A guest asks whether the barbecue shrimp is smoky. What is the true answer?
questions.answer: No: it is a buttery, peppery pan sauce
distractors: Yes, it is smoked over pecan wood first
Yes, glazed with a sweet tomato sauce
Lightly: grilled, then tossed in hot sauce
questions.why: New Orleans barbecue shrimp is never barbecued; the name covers a pan sauce of butter, pepper, Worcestershire, garlic and lemon.

questions.q: Why do cooks leave the heads on for barbecue shrimp?
questions.answer: Their fat enriches the butter sauce
distractors: They keep the shrimp from curling
They make the shrimp cook faster
They stop the sauce from splitting
questions.why: The fat in the heads melts into the butter as the shrimp cook, giving the sauce depth that peeled shrimp cannot.

questions.q: About how much cold butter goes with 450 g (1 lb) of head-on shrimp?
questions.why: About 115 g of butter makes enough glossy sauce to coat the shrimp and soak the bread without drowning them.

questions.q: What makes a barbecue shrimp sauce split into a pool of grease?
questions.answer: Boiling it after the butter goes in
distractors: Cooking the shrimp in their shells
questions.why: The sauce is a pan emulsion; boiling or sitting drives the butter out of suspension, so it is finished off the boil and served at once.

questions.q: When are the shrimp for barbecue shrimp done?
distractors: Shells black and the flesh firm and dry
Flesh still grey and clear at the centre
After 20 minutes at a rolling boil
questions.why: Large shrimp take 2 to 4 minutes in the pan and finish in the sauce; pulled when just opaque they stay tender, and seafood is cooked to 63°C (145°F).

questions.q: Which restaurant is credited, by its family's account, with creating barbecue shrimp?
questions.why: The family tells of a regular describing a Chicago shrimp dish in 1954 and the Uptown kitchen making its own version.

questions.q: What should arrive at the table with a bowl of barbecue shrimp?
questions.answer: Hot French bread, a bib and a bowl for shells
distractors: Steamed rice and a ladle of seafood gumbo
A fork and a fish knife, nothing more
Chilled cocktail sauce and saltine crackers
questions.why: The shrimp are peeled by hand and the sauce is the point, so bread for mopping and something for the shells come with it.

questions.q: On which Brennan's dish will a guest meet the New Orleans barbecue sauce at breakfast and lunch?
questions.why: The Louisiana Oysters carry the sauce at breakfast and lunch; at dinner it is on the Louisiana BBQ Lobster of the tasting.

questions.q: A guest asks whether the sauce on the Louisiana Oysters has anchovy in it. What do you do?
questions.answer: Ask the kitchen before they order
distractors: Judge it from the colour of the sauce
Tell them to scrape the sauce off
Read them the menu line and move on
questions.why: The house recipe is not published, and Worcestershire is traditionally made with anchovy, so the kitchen answers before the order goes in; a server never guesses.

entries.title: Blackening
entries.summary: Blackening is Paul Prudhomme's method: a fillet dipped in melted butter, coated in a paprika-led spice blend and seared in a dry cast-iron pan heated past smoking, so the spices toast to a dark crust while the inside stays moist.
entries.guest: Blackened means coated in a spice blend and seared in a very hot iron pan: a dark, spiced crust outside, moist inside. It is blackened, never burnt.

paras: Blackening is a young technique, created by the chef Paul Prudhomme at K-Paul's Louisiana Kitchen in the French Quarter around 1980. A fish fillet, classically redfish, is dipped in melted butter, coated thickly in a paprika-led spice blend and laid in a cast-iron pan heated dry until it is past smoking. In a couple of minutes a side the butter and spices toast into a dark, almost black crust while the fish inside stays moist.
Blackened is not burnt: burnt is bitter and acrid, blackened is toasty, spiced and savoury, and the difference is heat and speed.

Choose fillets of even thickness, about 1.25 cm (1/2 inch), so the inside cooks through in the time the crust takes to form; a thick fillet burns outside before it is done. Heat a heavy cast-iron pan dry over the highest flame for about 10 minutes, until it smokes hard and the surface is well above 260°C (500°F). No oil goes into the pan: the butter on the fish is the only fat.

Dip each fillet in melted butter, then press the spice blend onto both sides in an even, generous coat. Lay it in the pan away from you. Cook about 2 minutes, until the underside is dark and crusted, turn it once, spoon a little melted butter over the top and cook 1 to 2 minutes more. Fish is done at 63°C (145°F), when it flakes at the thickest part. Serve at once, crust up.

The blend is led by paprika. A common working proportion, by volume, is 3 parts sweet paprika and 2 to 2.5 parts salt to 1 part each of onion powder, garlic powder and cayenne, three-quarters of a part each of white and black pepper, and half a part each of dried thyme and oregano. Paprika gives the colour and toasts to the dark crust; cayenne and the peppers give heat; the herbs give a savoury, almost smoky note. Sugar has no place in it: sugar burns before the fish is cooked.

Blackening makes a great deal of smoke, and that is the method working: butter and spices meeting iron above 260°C (500°F). Restaurants do it under a strong extraction hood; at home it is best done outdoors on a burner, which is why home kitchens fill with smoke and set off alarms. Keep a lid beside the pan, never throw water on burning butter, and handle the iron with a dry cloth: it stays fiercely hot long after the flame is off.

A bitter, burnt crust means the fish stayed on too long, often because it was cut too thick, or the last batch's burnt residue was left in the pan. A grey, soggy coating comes from a cool or crowded pan. Fish that sticks and tears was turned too early; fish raw at the centre was cut too thick.

Blackened redfish became a national craze in the 1980s. That demand, with heavy commercial netting, drove red drum, the redfish, down hard. By the late 1980s federal waters of the Gulf were closed to red drum harvest, and Louisiana had closed its own commercial fishery; red drum is now a game fish there, for anglers rather than the market. Redfish on a menu today is farmed or legally caught elsewhere, and cooks blacken drum, catfish, chicken and vegetables too.

At Brennan's the method goes on tofu. The Blackened Tofu, a dinner entrée, is Tien Dat tofu, made fresh across the river by a local Vietnamese maker, blackened to a dark, spiced crust and set over Two Brooks Farm rice grits with preserved shiitake mushrooms. Because the classic method uses butter, and the rice grits may be cooked with stock, the house asks every server to check with the kitchen before calling the dish vegan.

Describe blackened food as a dark, spiced crust from a very hot iron pan, moist inside, warm with spice rather than fiery. Tell a guest who fears burnt food that the dark colour is toasted paprika and herbs. The Blackened Tofu runs to moderate spice; a guest wary of heat should hear that, and the kitchen can say more. Blackened is a method, not a sauce.

ratios.label: Spice blend, by volume
ratios.value: 3 paprika, 2 to 2.5 salt, 1 each onion powder, garlic powder and cayenne, three-quarters each white and black pepper, half each thyme and oregano

ratios.label: Heating the dry pan
ratios.value: About 10 minutes over the highest heat

ratios.label: Cooking time
ratios.value: About 2 minutes, turn once, then 1 to 2 minutes more

temps.label: The dry cast-iron pan, well above

faults.cause: Left on the heat too long, usually because the fillet was too thick, or burnt spice and butter from the last batch left in the pan.
faults.fix: Use fillets about 1.25 cm (1/2 inch) thick, cook about 2 minutes a side, and wipe the pan out between batches.

faults.cause: A cool pan, or too many fillets at once.
faults.fix: Cook one or two fillets at a time in a pan heated past smoking.

faults.cause: Turned before the crust had formed.
faults.fix: Leave it until the crust releases from the iron, then turn once.

faults.cause: The fillet was too thick for the short cook.
faults.fix: Split a thick fillet into two thinner ones before coating it.
Work under a powerful hood, or outdoors on a burner.

brennans.how: The Blackened Tofu takes Prudhomme's method to local tofu, a dark spiced crust over rice grits with preserved shiitake; the classic method uses butter, so check with the kitchen before calling it vegan.

cards.front: What is the blackening method?
cards.back: Prudhomme's method: a fillet dipped in melted butter, coated in a paprika-led spice blend and seared in a dry cast-iron pan heated past smoking.

cards.front: What is the difference between blackened and burnt?
cards.back: Blackened spices toast to a dark, savoury crust in a couple of minutes; burnt food is bitter. Heat and speed make the difference.

cards.front: Who created blackening, where and when?
cards.back: Paul Prudhomme, at K-Paul's Louisiana Kitchen in the French Quarter, around 1980.

cards.front: How hot is the pan for blackening, and what goes in it first?
cards.back: A dry cast-iron pan heated about 10 minutes until it smokes hard, well above 260°C (500°F); no oil, only the butter on the fish.

cards.front: What is in a blackening spice blend?
cards.back: Paprika first, then cayenne, black and white pepper, garlic and onion powder, dried thyme and oregano, and salt.

cards.front: Why does a blackening blend leave out sugar?
cards.back: Sugar burns at these temperatures before the fish is cooked, turning the crust bitter.

cards.front: Why are fillets for blackening cut about 1.25 cm (1/2 inch) thick?
cards.back: So the inside cooks through in the few minutes the crust takes; a thick fillet burns outside before it is done.

cards.front: How long does a blackened fillet cook, and when is it done?
cards.back: About 2 minutes on the first side and 1 to 2 on the second, until it flakes and reaches 63°C (145°F).

cards.front: Why is blackening done outdoors or under a strong hood?
cards.back: Butter and spices on iron above 260°C (500°F) make heavy smoke, which fills a home kitchen and sets off alarms.

cards.front: What did the blackened redfish craze do to Gulf redfish?
cards.back: Demand and heavy netting drove the stock down; by the late 1980s federal waters were closed to red drum harvest and Louisiana had closed its commercial fishery.

cards.front: Where is blackening on the Brennan's menu, and what must a server check?
cards.back: On the Blackened Tofu at dinner; the classic method uses butter, so check with the kitchen before calling the dish vegan.

questions.q: Which chef created blackening at his French Quarter restaurant around 1980?
questions.why: Prudhomme created blackening at K-Paul's Louisiana Kitchen, and blackened redfish made the method famous across the country.

questions.q: What goes into the cast-iron pan before the fish is laid in?
distractors: A thin film of olive oil
questions.why: The butter on the coated fillet is the only fat; oil or butter in a pan that hot would burn and flare.

questions.q: What separates a blackened crust from a burnt one?
questions.answer: Very high heat and a short cook
distractors: A long cook over low heat
A sugar glaze on the fish
A coat of flour under the spices
questions.why: In a pan past smoking the spices toast to a dark crust in a couple of minutes; left on the heat much longer, they turn bitter.

questions.q: Which spice leads a blackening blend?
questions.why: Paprika makes up the largest share; it gives the colour and toasts to the dark crust, with cayenne and the peppers for heat.

questions.q: Why does a blackening spice blend leave out sugar?
questions.answer: It would burn before the fish cooked
distractors: It would stop the spices toasting
It would keep the fish from flaking
It would turn the crust pale
questions.why: At pan temperatures well above 260°C (500°F) sugar turns bitter and black long before the fillet is done.

questions.q: Why do cooks blacken thin fillets of even thickness?
questions.answer: The inside cooks before the crust burns
distractors: Thin fillets soak up more of the butter
Thick fillets will not take spice
questions.why: The crust forms in a few minutes, so the fillet must be thin enough, about 1.25 cm (1/2 inch), to cook through in that time.

questions.q: Why is blackening done under a strong hood or outdoors?
distractors: The pan must be cooled by wind
questions.why: Butter and spices meeting iron well above 260°C (500°F) smoke hard, enough to fill a home kitchen and set off alarms.

questions.q: What followed the blackened redfish craze of the 1980s?
questions.answer: Closures of the commercial redfish fishery
distractors: A boom in Louisiana redfish exports
A ban on blackening in restaurants
questions.why: Demand and heavy netting drove red drum down; by the late 1980s federal waters were closed to its harvest and Louisiana had closed its commercial fishery.

questions.q: Why does a Brennan's server check with the kitchen before calling the Blackened Tofu vegan?
distractors: The menu lists it as a fish dish
Tofu must be cooked to order
The spice blend is always sweet
questions.why: Blackening traditionally dips the food in melted butter, and the rice grits may be cooked with stock, so the kitchen confirms how tonight's dish is made before anyone promises.
